# Temple Scroll — Reader's Guide

---

## At a Glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Attribution** | Anonymous; the text presents itself as direct speech of God to Moses — the only Dead Sea Scroll to do so throughout |
| **Actual Composition** | Core material drawn from earlier sources; final compilation c. 150–125 BCE, possibly during the Hasmonean period; some scholars argue a pre-Qumran origin with later sectarian editing |
| **Language** | Hebrew (deliberately archaic, imitating the register of the Pentateuch; some linguistic features suggest the author worked in a Pentateuchal idiom consciously) |
| **Audience** | The Qumran community and/or a broader reform movement within Second Temple Judaism; possibly also polemical — aimed at challenging the Jerusalem establishment's Temple practice |
| **Genre** | Rewritten Torah; the longest Dead Sea Scroll; presents itself as a direct Mosaic revelation, effectively a sixth book of Moses |
| **Length** | 67 columns; approximately 8.15 meters long when unrolled — the longest of all the scrolls from the Judean desert |
| **In One Sentence** | The Temple Scroll rewrites and expands the Pentateuch in God's own voice to prescribe a Temple of unprecedented scale and purity, a 364-day solar festival calendar, halakhic laws more stringent than the Masoretic text, and a constitutional monarchy strictly subordinated to divine law — presenting an alternative Torah for an alternative Israel. |

---

## Sections Overview

**Columns 2–13: The Festival Calendar and Sacrificial Laws**
The scroll opens (after a damaged beginning that may have contained a covenant ceremony) with a systematic reorganization of the sacrificial calendar. The Pentateuchal festivals — Passover, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, First Fruits of Grain (Pentecost/Shavuot), First Fruits of Wine, First Fruits of Oil, the Day of Atonement, Sukkot — are laid out in order. But the scroll adds two festivals entirely absent from the Masoretic Pentateuch: the Festival of New Wine and the Festival of New Oil, each celebrated fifty days after Pentecost on the Pentecost pattern. All of this is tied to the 364-day solar calendar the Qumran community used in place of the standard Jewish lunar calendar.

**Columns 3–13 (continued): Temple Architecture — the Inner Court**
The scroll describes an idealized Temple complex in three concentric rectangular courts. The innermost court contains the sanctuary proper, the altar, and facilities for priestly personnel. The specifications are given in immense detail: the dimensions of the gates (each named for one of the twelve tribes), the thickness of the walls, the placement of chambers, the materials to be used. The Temple described is larger than any temple that ever actually stood in Jerusalem — it could not physically fit on the Temple Mount as it existed. This is a visionary architecture, not an engineering blueprint, though it draws on real architectural knowledge.

**Columns 30–45: The Middle and Outer Courts**
The middle and outer courts expand the Temple compound to include facilities for laypeople, for the impure, and for the various categories of persons whose access to the sanctuary is graduated by their ritual status. The outer court is large enough to accommodate all of Israel for the major festivals. The scroll specifies the placement of stoas (colonnaded porticos) along the outer walls and the locations of facilities for cooking the festival sacrifices.

**Columns 45–51: Purity Laws**
These columns systematically tighten the purity regulations of the Pentateuch. Skin diseases (tzara'at), corpse impurity, bodily discharges — all are subject to more stringent requirements than in the Masoretic Torah. The holy city (Jerusalem, or rather the idealized city around the Temple) is treated as possessing the sanctity of the Temple camp in the wilderness — meaning the entire city must be maintained at the purity level the Pentateuch required only for the sanctuary area. Latrines must be constructed at a specific distance from the city (col. 46) — a ruling that has become one of the most discussed passages in DSS studies both for its stringency and for its possible resonance with John 19:41 (Jesus buried near the city gate, in a garden, on the day before Passover — precisely where the crucified would be placed according to col. 64).

**Columns 51–66: Deuteronomy Rewritten — Halakhic Laws**
These columns work through Deuteronomy 12–23 systematically, rewriting its laws in God's first-person voice, frequently tightening requirements, resolving ambiguities, and filling gaps. The treatment of idolatry, the festivals, the cities of refuge, judicial procedures, and family law are all addressed. The prohibition against intermarriage is expanded. The laws about warfare are elaborated.

**Columns 56–59: The Law of the King**
Deuteronomy 17:14–20's brief law of the king is vastly expanded. The king must be an Israelite (no foreigner). He must not multiply horses, wives, or gold (explicit quotation of Deuteronomy 17:16–17, now embedded in God's speech). He must have a standing army of twelve thousand soldiers selected from all the tribes. He must consult a council of twelve priests, twelve Levites, and twelve lay leaders before undertaking any major action. He may not make war without the approval of the high priest. The royal law has often been read as specifically anti-Hasmonean — the Hasmonean rulers combined the high priesthood with political and military authority in precisely the way the Temple Scroll forbids.

**Column 64: The Law of the Crucified Criminal**
The most discussed individual passage in the Temple Scroll. Deuteronomy 21:22–23 deals with hanging a criminal's body on a tree after execution. The Temple Scroll reinterprets (or rewrites) this passage to describe crucifixion as a mode of execution for a man who has "betrayed his people to a foreign nation" or cursed God. The passage is significant because: (1) it provides evidence that crucifixion was known and discussed in Jewish legal contexts before the Roman period; (2) Paul's argument in Galatians 3:13 that Christ became "a curse for us" by being "hung on a tree" (citing Deuteronomy 21:23) appears to engage with precisely this halakhic tradition; (3) the 4QpNahum scroll describes the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus crucifying 800 Pharisees, possibly under the legal framework this passage provides.

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Temple Scroll was written in a period when the Jerusalem Temple was physically standing, politically contested, and theologically central to Jewish identity — and when a significant portion of observant Jews believed it was being managed wrongly.

The Temple of the Second Temple period was Herod's Temple (rebuilt on the foundations of Zerubbabel's Temple). It was an enormous and magnificent structure by any measure. But for the Qumran community, it was doubly illegitimate: its priesthood was corrupt (not Zadokite), and its calendar was wrong (lunar rather than solar). Sacrifices offered on the wrong days, by illegitimate priests, in a building that did not meet divine specifications — for the Yahad, the Jerusalem Temple was not merely imperfect but actively invalid.

The Temple Scroll responded to this crisis by presenting God's definitive instructions for the true Temple, dictated directly to Moses at Sinai, and apparently lost or suppressed by the corrupt establishment. This rhetorical move — presenting a corrective text as the authentic Mosaic revelation — was available because the Pentateuch itself contains multiple accounts of Mosaic instruction, some in third-person narrative and some in direct divine speech, and significant tensions in the Torah's legal material were well known to scribal scholars.

The 364-day solar calendar is crucial to understanding the scroll's festival legislation. This calendar divides the year into four seasons of thirteen weeks each, with one additional day. Every feast falls on the same day of the week every year, and none of the major festivals can fall on the Sabbath (since the calendar is fixed). The lunar calendar used in Jerusalem meant that festivals shifted relative to the week, and in some years Passover or Pentecost would fall on the Sabbath — creating legal complications the Yahad considered scandalous. By the Qumran calendar, the Jerusalem Temple was celebrating Passover on the wrong day every year. That is not a minor liturgical disagreement; it invalidates the entire sacrificial system.

The Temple Scroll's idealized Temple had another function: it embodied a vision of Israel's eschatological future. The Temple described in cols. 3–45 is too large for the Jerusalem Temple Mount and too ideal for any historical construction. It corresponds in some respects to Ezekiel's visionary Temple in chapters 40–48. The scroll seems to present this Temple as what God will build when the age of corruption ends — the Temple of the new creation — while also providing halakhic legislation for a purified Temple that could be built now, if Israel would repent and live by the scroll's standards.

---

## Why This Text Was Written

The Temple Scroll's rhetorical strategy reveals its purpose. By putting its legislation in God's own voice — eliminating the narrative frame of Moses receiving and transmitting divine speech, and having God speak directly in the first person throughout — the scroll claims the highest possible authority for its halakhic rulings. Any disagreement is not disagreement with a human author but with God himself.

This suggests the scroll was written to resolve legal disputes. Second Temple Judaism was characterized by intense halakhic debate — the Pharisees, Sadducees, and various other groups disputed the correct interpretation of Mosaic law on hundreds of specific points. The Temple Scroll does not enter these debates; it ends them, by presenting God's unambiguous first-person ruling on every contested point.

The scroll also served as a counter-canon to the Jerusalem priestly establishment's interpretation of Torah. Where the Masoretic text was ambiguous, the Temple Scroll clarified — always in the direction of greater stringency. Where the Masoretic text gave the king authority, the Temple Scroll subjected him to priestly oversight. Where the Masoretic text's festival calendar could be observed on a lunar calendar, the Temple Scroll's comprehensive festival legislation required the solar calendar.

The royal law (cols. 56–59) in particular reads as a direct political argument. The Hasmonean rulers had accumulated the high priesthood, the kingship, and military command simultaneously — precisely the concentration of power the scroll forbids. Whether the scroll was composed as anti-Hasmonean polemic from the start or was read that way by the Qumran community, its political implications were clear.

---

## How to Read This Text

**Begin with the royal law (cols. 56–59) and the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:14–20.** Comparing them side by side is the fastest way to understand the Temple Scroll's method: it takes a brief Pentateuchal text, expands it dramatically, tightens its requirements, and adds legislation not present in the original. Then read 1 Samuel 8 (Israel's request for a king) and Ezekiel 44–46 (the prince's subordinate role in the restored Temple). The Temple Scroll participates in a long conversation about the proper relationship between royal and priestly authority.

**Read the purity laws (cols. 45–51) slowly and with attention to their logic.** The purity regulations are not arbitrary taboos but a systematic application of a single principle: the holiness of the Temple extends outward to its entire surrounding territory. The holy city is as holy as the Temple court; Israel's land is as holy as the holy city. This is a coherent theology, not just a list of rules. Compare Leviticus 15's regulations on bodily discharges and ask what it would mean to apply those regulations to an entire urban population.

**Notice what the scroll does with the first person throughout.** In the Pentateuch, God speaks in the first person in some passages ("I am the LORD your God who brought you out of Egypt...") and in the third person in others ("the LORD said to Moses, 'Say to the Israelites...'"). The Temple Scroll eliminates the third-person frame. "Moses" essentially disappears. God speaks directly about himself, about the Temple he wants built, about the laws he prescribes. This is a major literary and theological move. Ask: what effect does hearing these laws in God's first-person voice have on a reader who accepts the scroll's authority?

**Read column 64 with Galatians 3:10–14 and Deuteronomy 21:22–23 simultaneously.** The legal background of Paul's "curse" argument in Galatians requires understanding that Deuteronomy 21:23 was being actively interpreted and applied to the Roman practice of crucifixion in first-century Jewish legal circles. The Temple Scroll shows that this application was already underway.

---

## The Threads

**Hebrew Bible**
- **Deuteronomy 17 (the law of the king)**: The royal law in cols. 56–59 is the most dramatic expansion in the scroll. Deuteronomy's fifteen verses become several columns.
- **Deuteronomy 21:22–23 (hanging on a tree)**: Column 64's crucifixion law rewrites this passage in ways that directly anticipate NT interpretation.
- **Leviticus 12–15 (purity regulations)**: The scroll's purity laws (cols. 45–51) systematically intensify the Levitical material.
- **Ezekiel 40–48**: The architectural vision of the eschatological Temple — with its three courts, its tribal gates, its graduated purity zones — is the Temple Scroll's most important scriptural predecessor. Ezekiel's Temple is visionary and unrealized; the Temple Scroll provides the detailed halakhic specifications for building it.
- **Numbers 28–29 (festival offerings)**: The scroll's festival calendar (cols. 13–23) expands the Numbers sacrificial schedule while aligning it with the 364-day solar year.

**New Testament**
- **Galatians 3:10–14**: Paul's use of Deuteronomy 21:23 ("Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree") to interpret Jesus's crucifixion engages with the legal tradition attested in column 64. The Temple Scroll shows that the interpretation of this passage in relation to execution by crucifixion was a live legal debate before Paul's time.
- **Mark 11:15–17 (Cleansing of the Temple)**: Jesus's action in the Temple and his citation of Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 take on additional texture against the Temple Scroll's vision of what the Temple should be. For communities shaped by the Temple Scroll tradition, the Temple Jesus encountered was not merely ethically corrupted but structurally wrong.
- **John 2:13–22**: Jesus's statement that his body is the Temple ("destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it") echoes debates about Temple legitimacy that the Temple Scroll exemplifies.
- **Revelation 21:9–27**: The New Jerusalem that descends from heaven in Revelation 21 — with its twelve gates named for the twelve tribes, its perfect symmetry, its absence of a Temple building because God himself is its Temple — can be read as the eschatological fulfillment and transcendence of the visionary architecture in both Ezekiel 40–48 and the Temple Scroll.
- **Hebrews 9–10**: The argument that Jesus's sacrifice renders the entire Jerusalem sacrificial system obsolete engages with the question of Temple legitimacy from a different angle than the Temple Scroll, but the underlying question — what is the true Temple and the true sacrifice? — is shared.

**Other Dead Sea Scrolls**
- **4QMMT (Halakhic Letter)**: This letter from the community leadership to a Jerusalem authority sets out specific halakhic rulings — many of which agree with the Temple Scroll's more stringent positions. 4QMMT appears to be the specific legal brief that accompanied the community's initial separation; the Temple Scroll provides the fuller legislative framework.
- **Jubilees**: The book of Jubilees, multiple copies of which were found at Qumran and which the community regarded as authoritative, uses the same 364-day solar calendar as the Temple Scroll. It also presents its legislation as direct divine speech to Moses, through the mediation of the Angel of Presence. Jubilees and the Temple Scroll are parallel projects with different emphases.
- **1QS (Community Rule)**: The community's practical governance document; the Temple Scroll provides its vision of the ideal Temple and Israel that the community believes it is preparing for.
- **Damascus Document (CD)**: Contains multiple halakhic rulings that overlap with the Temple Scroll's legislation, suggesting the scroll was used as a halakhic reference across the broader movement.

**Other Ancient Texts**
- **Ezekiel the Tragedian** (a Jewish playwright, c. 2nd century BCE): His dramatization of the Exodus demonstrates that Second Temple Jews were engaged in creative rewriting of Pentateuchal narrative. The Temple Scroll is the most ambitious halakhic version of this same rewriting impulse.
- **Josephus, *Antiquities* III–IV**: Josephus's paraphrase of the Mosaic law also rewrites Pentateuchal legislation in a more systematic way than the MT, though in a very different rhetorical register. Both projects reflect the scribal impulse to clarify and systematize Torah.
- **The Letter of Aristeas**: The concern with Temple purity, priestly protocol, and the relationship between Jewish law and political authority reflected in this Alexandrian text provides context for the Temple Scroll's legislative agenda.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

**1. The scroll is simultaneously Torah and not Torah.**
The most disorienting feature of the Temple Scroll for a modern reader is its genre ambiguity. It presents itself as divine speech to Moses at Sinai — which is the same claim the Pentateuch makes for itself. But it expands, modifies, and in some places contradicts the Masoretic Pentateuch. Was the community that valued this scroll treating it as equivalent to the Torah? As supplementary to it? As a corrective reading of it? Scholars disagree. What is clear is that the scroll occupied an authoritative status somewhere at or very near the top of the community's normative hierarchy, and its first-person divine voice was not an accident but a deliberate claim to the highest possible authority.

**2. The 364-day calendar is not an eccentricity — it is a theological rupture.**
For the Qumran community, the difference between the 364-day solar calendar and the Jerusalem lunar calendar was not a minor liturgical quibble. It was the difference between worshiping on the days God actually appointed and worshiping on the wrong days — which meant the Jerusalem Temple's sacrifices were offered at the wrong time and were therefore invalid. The calendar division placed the entire community in permanent, irresolvable conflict with the Jerusalem establishment. Every Passover they ate lamb on a different day than Jerusalem. Every Yom Kippur they fasted while Jerusalem feasted. The Temple Scroll's comprehensive festival legislation is at the same time a comprehensive indictment of Jerusalem's practice.

**3. The three-court Temple is a graduated map of holiness, not just an architecture.**
The concentric courts of the Temple Scroll's ideal sanctuary are not arbitrary architectural choices. They encode a theology of graduated holiness: the innermost court (priests only), the middle court (Israelite men), the outer court (women and proselytes, in some readings). Each gate is named for a tribe, distributing the entire people of Israel spatially around the sanctuary. The impure and the excluded are kept at specified distances. The Temple is a diagram of the social and spiritual order of Israel — a map of who stands where before God. Reading the architectural specification is reading an ecclesiology.

**4. The anti-Hasmonean polemic was politically dangerous.**
Scholars who read the royal law as anti-Hasmonean should appreciate the courage required to write and preserve such a document. Alexander Jannaeus (103–76 BCE) was not a tolerant ruler — he crucified eight hundred Pharisees after a political uprising. A text claiming divine authority for the proposition that the king must not hold the high priesthood, must not wage war without priestly approval, and must not accumulate personal wealth was not politically neutral. The decision to write the legislation in God's own first-person voice rather than as human commentary may have been partly a protective move: it is harder to prosecute an author for sedition when the author claims to be transcribing divine speech.

**5. Column 64 changed the study of crucifixion.**
Before the Temple Scroll was published (Yigael Yadin's edition appeared in 1977, though the scroll was acquired in 1967 during the Six-Day War), scholars generally assumed that crucifixion as a legal penalty was a Roman invention applied to Jewish subjects. Column 64 showed that Jewish legal scholars had already engaged with the Deuteronomy 21:22–23 "hanging on a tree" passage as a possible authorization for a form of execution that closely resembles crucifixion. This did not make crucifixion "Jewish," but it showed that the legal context for crucifixion — including the interpretation of Deuteronomy 21:23 that Paul uses in Galatians 3:13 — was actively debated within Jewish halakhic circles before and alongside the New Testament period.

**6. The scroll was not found in a clay jar — it was found in a shoe box.**
The acquisition story of the Temple Scroll is one of the more colorful episodes in modern archaeology. The scroll was not discovered in an orderly excavation. It was purchased by Yigael Yadin from an antiquities dealer named Kando in 1967, immediately after the Israeli capture of the West Bank in the Six-Day War. For years before Yadin's acquisition it had been owned by a Jordanian antiquities dealer named Kando, stored under the floorboards of his house in Bethlehem, partially damaged, and rolled up in a shoe box. Its fragmentary condition in some columns reflects this careless storage. Despite this, it is the longest and one of the best-preserved major Dead Sea Scrolls.

---

## Why This Text Isn't in Your Bible

The Temple Scroll raises the question of canon inclusion in a particularly sharp form because it is, in a sense, the text that most aggressively claimed to be Scripture. It presents itself in the same literary form as Mosaic Torah — divine speech to Moses at Sinai. If a reader accepted its authority, it would function as a corrective and supplementary sixth book of the Pentateuch.

It is not in any biblical canon for several reasons. First, it was a sectarian document belonging to the Yahad or a related reform movement. The community that preserved it was destroyed in 68 CE, before the text could circulate widely enough to influence either the rabbinic or the Christian canonical process. Second, its claims contradicted the Masoretic text in ways that made acceptance of both impossible: if the Temple Scroll's festival legislation was authoritative, Jerusalem's entire sacrificial calendar was wrong, and the legitimacy of the Temple establishment was undermined. No mainstream group could accept a text that implied this conclusion while also maintaining any connection to the Jerusalem Temple tradition.

Third, the rabbinic canon formed after 70 CE around the principle of stabilizing the Masoretic text and the oral traditions that interpreted it. A document claiming to be an alternative first-person Torah, with a different calendar and more stringent halakhah, fit neither the stabilizing project nor the oral tradition framework. The rabbis who compiled the Mishnah were aware of texts like this and explicitly excluded them from consideration. Sanhedrin 10:1's list of those who have no share in the world to come includes one who says "Torah is not from heaven" — meaning, in context, one who claims a text other than the received Torah is the authoritative divine word.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **c. 586–515 BCE** | Babylonian exile and return; the Ezekiel 40–48 Temple vision composed; no Second Temple yet built to fulfill it |
| **515 BCE** | Second Temple (Zerubbabel's Temple) dedicated; modest, without the Ark of the Covenant |
| **168–164 BCE** | Antiochus IV desecrates the Temple; Maccabean revolt; rededication (Hanukkah) |
| **c. 150–125 BCE** | Temple Scroll composed in final form; likely the Hasmonean high priesthood is the immediate polemical target |
| **152 BCE** | Jonathan Maccabee assumes high priesthood; Qumran community's founding crisis |
| **103–76 BCE** | Alexander Jannaeus rules; crucifies 800 Pharisees; anti-Hasmonean polemic of the royal law is most relevant here |
| **20 BCE – 64 CE** | Herod the Great and his successors rebuild the Temple on a massive scale — a Temple far grander than Zerubbabel's but not the Temple the scroll prescribes |
| **c. 50 BCE – 68 CE** | 11Q19 (our scroll) copied; preserved at Qumran |
| **66–70 CE** | First Jewish Revolt; Temple destroyed 70 CE — the Temple the scroll critiqued no longer stands |
| **68 CE** | Qumran destroyed; scroll hidden in Cave 11 |
| **1956 CE** | Cave 11 discovered (one of the last caves found in systematic excavation) |
| **1967 CE** | Temple Scroll acquired by Yigael Yadin during and after the Six-Day War |
| **1977 CE** | Yadin publishes the critical edition in Hebrew; English translation follows in 1983 |

---

*HESED notes: The Temple Scroll is the most legally demanding of the major DSS texts, and it rewards patient reading in dialogue with its Pentateuchal sources. The single most illuminating exercise for understanding this text is to read Deuteronomy 17 alongside cols. 56–59, then Leviticus 14–15 alongside cols. 45–51, noting both where the scroll expands and where it tightens. The theological question the scroll poses — what does the true Temple of God look like, and what kind of holiness does it require of those who approach it? — is one the New Testament also asks, from the very different angle of Jesus as the new Temple and the community of believers as the living sanctuary. The Temple Scroll shows that these are not new questions invented by the early church but ancient questions that Jewish communities were already asking with great intensity.*
